entries.title: Benchmarking VLM Medical Hallucination across 5 Modalities
entries.abstract: Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) within the medical domain remain a difficult and not well-understood problem, and it is still unclear where these models break down. Although several benchmarks targeting medical hallucination have been introduced, they often lack broad coverage across different medical imaging modalities. We introduce Multi-Med, a medical hallucination benchmark containing 1,000 image-question pairs spanning five distinct modalities. Using this benchmark, we perform an in-depth experimental study of 10 widely used VLMs across five modalities and four question categories. Our findings indicate that model performance differs substantially depending on the imaging modality and question type, and that the differences among the best-performing models are not statistically significant.

entries.title: Error Direction of Large Language Models on Medical Multiple-Response Questions: Opportunity-Standardized Benchmark Study.
entries.abstract:
Background

Large language models (LLMs) attain high accuracy on medical examinations, yet evaluations rely predominantly on single-best-answer multiple-choice questions and report only overall accuracy. Multiple-response items, termed X-type in China, require selecting every correct option and remain understudied. Whether models err by omitting correct options or by commissioning incorrect ones has yet to be assessed within an opportunity-standardized framework.

Objective

This study aimed to quantify the accuracy penalty of multiple-response (X-type) items relative to single-select items and to determine, after standardizing for the unequal numbers of correct and incorrect options, whether LLMs lean toward omission or commission.

Methods

We analyzed 1644 text-based items from 10 examination cohorts (2017-2026) of the Chinese National Postgraduate Entrance Examination in Clinical Medicine, comprising 1344 single-select items of types A1, A2, A3, and B, and 300 X-type items. Five LLMs, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Doubao Seed-2.1-pro, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini-3.6 Flash, were tested zero-shot bilingually, yielding 16,440 planned responses. Item-type effects were estimated using generalized estimating equations with cluster-robust standard errors, adjusting for model, language, discipline, and cohort. Opportunity-standardized error direction was analyzed 2 ways: an option-level model treating each option as 1 judgment record and the omission-bias index.

Results

Of 16,440 planned responses, 16,426 (99.91%) were evaluable. X-type accuracy (2527/3000, 84.23%) was markedly below single-select accuracy (12,990/13,426, 96.75%; adjusted odds ratio at GPT-5.6 Sol in Chinese 0.17, 95% CI 0.11-0.26; P<.001), a gap of 12.52 percentage points observed and 13.55 adjusted, with no statistically significant item type × model or item type × language interaction (P=.19 and P=.82). Raw counts suggested more strict omissions (245/3000, 8.17%) than overselections (201/3000, 6.70%), but X-type items averaged 2.79 correct vs 1.21 incorrect options per item, a 2.3-fold imbalance in error opportunities. After opportunity standardization, the per-opportunity false-selection rate was 6.69% (242/3620), roughly twice the 3.57% per-opportunity omission rate (299/8380; rate ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.28-2.74; adjusted odds ratio at the reference model and language 0.38, 95% CI 0.20-0.70; P=.002), so the tilt is modest on the absolute scale and close to 2-fold on the relative scale. Strict omission showed no between-model difference (all Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons, P≥.46).

Conclusions

LLMs incur a substantial accuracy penalty on medical multiple-response items. The apparent omission dominance in raw counts is an artifact of answer-key opportunity imbalance; after opportunity standardization, models show a commission tilt that is modest on the absolute scale (3.12 percentage points per opportunity) and close to 2-fold on the relative scale, and that holds in every model-language condition and in the answer-key stratum whose opportunity base is exactly balanced. Medical LLM benchmarks should report accuracy stratified by item type and error direction on an opportunity-standardized basis.

entries.title: Diagnostic specificity of a retrieval augmented language model on complex clinical cases: a retrospective benchmark study
entries.abstract: Background Diagnostic benchmarks can reward recognition of a disease family without requiring the specificity of the final diagnosis. We evaluated the separation between broad diagnostic concordance and strict diagnostic correctness in a retrieval augmented language model. Methods This retrospective benchmark evaluated MediDx AI, which couples Claude Sonnet 4.6 with retrieval from seven biomedical sources without fine-tuning, on presentation-only text from 100 consecutive published Massachusetts General Hospital Case Records, issued from 26 October 2023 to 11 June 2026. Published expert discussions, final diagnoses, source tables and images were withheld. Five ranked suggestions were adjudicated under broad concordance and strict correct, partial or incorrect scoring. Case-level proportions and Wilson 95% confidence intervals were calculated. A separate evaluation used 1,273 medical multiple-choice questions, counting unanswered questions as incorrect. Results Broad top-ranked concordance was 71% (95% confidence interval 61.5–79.0%), whereas 53% (43.3–62.5%) of top-ranked diagnoses were strictly correct; 19% were partial and 28% incorrect. Within five suggestions, broad concordance was 88% and strict correctness was 63%. The 18 broadly concordant but partial top-ranked diagnoses accounted for the difference between the two top-ranked outcomes. Failures included missed causative organisms, rare neoplasms and structural conditions; partial responses often omitted an underlying mechanism or a component of a multicomponent diagnosis. Medical question-answering accuracy was 86.5% across all submitted questions, compared with 92.0% among parseable responses; response coverage was 94.0%. Conclusions Broad diagnostic concordance and strict diagnostic correctness describe different aspects of performance. Reporting both, alongside ranked inclusion and response completion, exposes information concealed by aggregate accuracy. These results do not establish the incremental benefit of retrieval or clinical effectiveness, which require controlled evaluation.

entries.title: From benchmarking to application: a scalable mitochondrial DNA analysis and variant identification framework for whole-genome sequencing
entries.abstract:
Purpose: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants are implicated in a wide range of diseases. The increasing availability of whole-genome sequencing enables mtDNA analysis in large-scale clinical and population studies. However, optimal tools for accurate variant detection from short-read data remain unclear.

Methods:

We systematically benchmarked four scalable mtDNA variant calling tools: MitoHPC, mtSwirl, mity, and mtDNA-Server 2. Using 1000 Genomes Project (1KG) data and simulations across diverse haplogroups, we evaluated performance in detecting homoplasmic and heteroplasmic variants. Using the optimal tool, we built MARVel (https://github.com/bahlolab/MARVel), an integrated workflow combining variant calling, automated quality-control reporting, and interactive variant curation, including an mtDNA principal component reference from 1KG that captures haplogroup structure and enables projection of external cohorts. We then applied MARVel to an independent ataxia cohort to assess research utility.

Results:

MitoHPC and mtSwirl showed the strongest overall performance, particularly in non-European populations, with MitoHPC preferred for its ease of implementation. mity excelled in detecting low variant allele frequency single nucleotide variants (SNVs) but underperformed for insertions/deletions and showed inconsistent multi-nucleotide polymorphism normalisation. mtDNA-Server 2 maximised SNV sensitivity but had a higher false-positive rate and missed variants in the MT-RNR2 region. Applying MARVel (MitoHPC) to the ataxia cohort recovered known pathogenic mtDNA variants and identified additional candidates for investigation.

Conclusion:

We provide guidance for mtDNA tool selection in large-scale sequencing studies, along with a reproducible benchmarking framework for future evaluation as methods evolve. We also developed MARVel to facilitate disease-associated mtDNA variant discovery and reporting, supporting robust and scalable mtDNA analysis.

entries.title: MaskRet-Oto: region-conditioned evidence retrieval and calibration for otoscopic image classification and selective referral.
entries.abstract: Digital otoscopy is a compact biomedical imaging modality, but retrospective image-classification results can be distorted by duplicate content, acquisition-domain cues, uncertain confidence, and dataset prevalence. We revised the framework as MaskRet-Oto, a region-conditioned evidence-retrieval and calibration pipeline rather than a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. The working archive contained 3000 RGB otoscopic images in five approximately balanced categories. Exact-hash auditing identified 78 duplicated files; the remaining 2922 images formed 1956 within-class perceptual-hash groups that were kept intact across training (n= 2046), validation (n= 438), and test (n= 438) partitions. Because patient identifiers were unavailable, this procedure controls only exact/near-duplicate image leakage and cannot establish patient-independent evaluation; different views from the same patient or examination could remain in different splits. The soft central field-of-view operator retained 70.9% of image support and is now described as a predefined region-conditioning prior, not as empirical proof that shortcut learning was prevented. On the internal image-level test set, the compact 64 × 64 CNN pipeline achieved 98.17% accuracy (95% bootstrap confidence interval 96.80%-99.32%), 98.23% macro-F1, MCC 0.977, and macro-AUC 0.9994. Training-only visual retrieval reached 99.54% top-5 recall. The source-tagged textual memory contains 15 curated statements retrieved by TF-IDF; no language model is used and the component is not presented as a clinical knowledge base or RAG. Retrieval fusion did not improve top-1 accuracy; its role is limited to exposing similar training cases, attaching source-tagged evidence, and contributing a small additional calibration change after temperature scaling. Selective prediction concentrated all observed errors in the lowest-confidence decile in this same test set, but this is a post hoc internal utility surrogate, not a clinical-utility validation. The nearly balanced benchmark distribution also means that calibration values should not be interpreted as real-world disease-risk probabilities. Patient-level, device-diverse, prevalence-aware, and prospective validation with stronger standard backbones is required before clinical use.
